meta.title: Pharmy Case Study: One Searchable Clinical Trial Platform | Viesigners
meta.description: How Charles-Erick BG led the UX of one searchable clinical trial platform and tested a two-step form on real traffic.

sections.lead: With the project team, I led the UX and CRO of a clinical trial platform, from analysis to the winning version: 48% more visitors reached the form, contact requests came from prequalified people, and the client got a data-driven roadmap.

items.t: A pharmaceutical company. Pharmy is a fictional name; the real one is under NDA.
Encourage potential participants to send their personal information through the qualification form, so the client’s team could focus on qualified candidates.
I worked closely with a consultant hired by the client: I advised and he approved. We also had regular touch points with the client’s project lead for final validation.

Analysis, hypothesis, A/B methodology, measurement, information architecture and interface recommendations through wireframes. I also guided the project team from ideation to technical validation and advised the graphic designer, who created the final UI.

impact.t: more visitors reached the qualification form: 5.6% to 8.3% of visits.
potential gain in qualification forms sent per visit: 1.95% to 2.34%.
impact.note: Note: small sample, not statistically significant.

impact.t: data-driven next tests for the client, drawn from analytics and session recordings.

sections.label: The friction
sections.h2: Two problems kept people *from joining a trial*

items.p: The client’s focus groups started this project. People were missing the information they needed to trust the platform and the process, and they needed a clinic close enough to reach.

items.h: A form that felt too long
items.p: My audit showed that people didn’t fill in the qualification form and left, so the client relied only on those who finished it.
The client’s team received forms from unqualified people and lost time following up on them.
Each study had its own microsite, so the same general information was repeated on each one and harder to keep up to date.
Group the microsites in one searchable platform, like Airbnb for clinical trials, with the general information people needed in one place. That would also make updates easier for the client’s team.

items.h: Test a new version on real traffic
items.p: From my Google Analytics, Hotjar and form audit findings, we hypothesized that two changes would get more people to send their information: one study page built around their main objections, and a form split in two steps.

sections.label: Approach
prose: **I started from the Google Analytics and Hotjar data.** The focus groups the client ran before the project backed up what I found. I then framed the test hypothesis, wrote the A/B methodology and set the indicators and measurement plan with the client’s team.

items.h: Split the form in two steps to receive only qualified forms
items.p: A prescreener came first, then contact details for people who qualified.

notes.v: The existing form against the two-step form I proposed.
My audit showed people left the long form before finishing. A first step without personal details asks less up front and keeps people in the funnel.

More build work, including a back button between the steps. Of the people who reached the form, fewer sent it in version B (28% vs 35%). But since more people reached it, submissions still rose overall.

shots.label: Wireframe: form step 1 on mobile
shots.alt: Mobile wireframe of the first form step: a two-step stepper, eligibility questions and a See if you qualify button

items.h: Give people who don’t qualify a reason to stay
items.p: People who didn’t qualify could join a community through the newsletter.

notes.v: The newsletter kept them in the loop, so the client could reach them again later and propose new trials better suited to them.

items.h: Answer objections before asking people to search
items.p: A strategic homepage sequence answered objections and showed people they weren’t alone. Version B of the A/B test also changed the study page.

notes.v: Land people on the map search, with explanations behind links.
Unanswered objections stop people from acting, as the focus groups showed. Simple pages on conditions, terms and trials were also easier to maintain.
Search came almost first on the homepage, but stayed first in the menu for people ready to act.

items.h: Make distance visible with a map
items.p: People search by condition and location, and see the trials on a map.

notes.v: A filtered list, or one marker per condition, which would have been too cluttered since a clinic could run several studies.
The focus groups showed people had to travel to the clinic, and acceptable distance varied by condition. I grouped trials by clinic, inspired by Airbnb and real estate map apps.
It was much harder to design and build. With the developer, I used the map library’s built-in clustering, which performed better and was simpler.

sections.label: A design challenge that arose
prose: Merging the microsites into one platform meant two navigation systems on the same pages.

**I explored two options:** stacking the menus, or swapping to the microsite menu with a back button. Stacking adds cognitive load. Swapping is lighter, but “Back” means nothing to people who land directly on a microsite.
I stacked slim menus that hide on scroll, with comfortable touch targets. On mobile, the hamburger menu handled the way back.

sections.label: What real users did
sections.h2: What the A/B test *showed, and what it didn’t*

reads.p: Version B did better at convincing people to check their eligibility, a result that stays statistically significant on this sample, though narrowly. It also sorted people: 47% of its submissions came from prequalified candidates, who then shared contact details, while the others could join the community.

On this small sample, the +20% isn’t statistically significant. Clicks on the form buttons also trended the other way, so some people may have reached the form directly. The report also flags test visits and configuration bugs. I flagged the sample size at the time, and the client decided to move forward anyway.
Version B changed the study page and the form together, so the test can’t credit either one alone.
Hotjar recordings suggested friction on some prescreener fields, while qualified people filled in the contact form easily. On the not-qualified page, people mostly read the title and left.

stats.sub: A: content on two pages · B: content on one page
A: full form · B: prescreener only

items.h: A clear call on version B
items.p: I recommended keeping version B because it brought 48% more visitors to the form, and I was upfront about what the sample couldn’t confirm. That gave the client a decision it could trust.

I turned what people struggled with into a roadmap. They hit friction on prescreener fields, so I proposed simpler ones. Not-qualified visitors read the title and left, so I moved the community form to the top of a shorter page. I also proposed fewer calls to action on the study page.
I’d push for more traffic or a longer test. It ran for three months, but too few people reached the forms to confirm the submission result.

The contact step would be sent as soon as people moved to step 2, and the qualification questions would come in smaller chunks, so the form feels lighter. People who stopped after the contact step would receive an email sequence inviting them to finish, so the client’s team wouldn’t spend time on incomplete forms.
Right under the homepage banner, a section would show we understand people’s situation before talking about our solution (joining the trial participants community).
